issues.legal_issue: A separately let portion of a building is not necessarily a separate building for a claim for additional accommodation.
material_facts: The landlords occupied the first floor of a building as their residence, while the tenant occupied the ground floor as a godown.
The court found that the ground floor was not a distinct and separate unit from the rest of the building.
issues.conclusion: The landlords could seek eviction under Section 10(3)(c) because the building was to be treated as one integrated unit for that claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(2) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 defines a building to include a separately let part, but makes that definition subject to context. Section 10(3)(c), which concerns a landlord occupying part of a building and seeking the remaining part as additional accommodation, requires the building to be treated as an integrated unit where that is necessary to give effect to the provision. A construction that would render Section 10(3)(c) otiose should be avoided. The court approved Saraswathi Sriraman v. P.C.R. Chetty's Charities, Mohammed Jaffar v. Palaniappa Chettiar, and Chellammal v. Accommodation Controller.

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_procee: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant to obtain additional accommodation in a building the landlord partly occupies.
predicates.landlord_occupies_part_of_integrated_bui: The landlord occupies one part of a building that functions as an integrated structure.
predicates.tenant_occupies_remaining_part: The tenant occupies another part of that same building.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks additional accommodation from a tenant occupying another part of an integrated building, the tenant's portion may be treated as part of the same building.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking additional accommodation under Section 10(3)(c) may seek possession even when the tenant's use of the remaining part differs from the landlord's intended use.
material_facts: The landlords occupied part of the building for residence and sought the ground floor for additional residential accommodation.
The tenant used the ground floor as a godown for business goods.
issues.conclusion: The landlords could invoke Section 10(3)(c) for residential needs even though the tenant used the remaining part for a non-residential purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(c) applies to a landlord occupying part of a residential or non-residential building and permits an application against any tenant occupying the remaining part for additional residential or business accommodation, as the case may be. Its non-obstante clause overrides the restrictions in Section 10(3)(a)(i) and (iii), including the requirement that the tenant's use correspond to the landlord's need. The words “any tenant” and “as the case may be” do not impose a matching-use restriction. The court approved K. Parasuramaiah v. Lakshmamma and overruled Thirupathi v. Kanta Rao.

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_procee: A landlord seeks eviction to obtain additional accommodation in a building the landlord partly occupies.
predicates.landlord_occupies_part_of_building: The landlord occupies one part of the building from which additional accommodation is sought.
predicates.landlord_has_bona_fide_additional_accomm: The landlord genuinely needs additional accommodation for residential or business purposes.
predicates.tenant_uses_remaining_part_for_different: The tenant uses the remaining part for a purpose different from the landlord's intended use.

issues.definition: A landlord with a genuine need for additional accommodation may seek eviction from the remaining part even when the tenant uses it for a different purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Eviction for additional accommodation may be ordered when the landlord's bona fide need is established and the advantage to the landlord outweighs the hardship to the tenant.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found the landlords' need bona fide and found that the advantage to them outweighed the hardship to the tenant.
The landlords relied on limited residential space, the difficulty an elderly occupant had climbing stairs, and the growing need for a separate room for a child.
The tenant had a spacious multi-storey building adjoining the premises and another godown nearby.
issues.conclusion: The landlords were entitled to an order of eviction because their bona fide need was established and the advantage of eviction outweighed the tenant's hardship.
issues.legal_principle: The first proviso to Section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 requires the Controller to reject an application if the hardship to the tenant outweighs the advantage to the landlord. Once the landlord establishes bona fide need for additional accommodation and the advantage to the landlord outweighs the tenant's hardship, eviction may be ordered irrespective of other considerations.

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_procee: A landlord seeks eviction to obtain additional accommodation in a building the landlord partly occupies.
predicates.landlord_has_bona_fide_additional_accomm: The landlord genuinely needs additional accommodation for residential or business purposes.
predicates.landlord_advantage_outweighs_tenant_hard: The advantage to the landlord from eviction is greater than the hardship the eviction would cause the tenant.

issues.definition: When a landlord genuinely needs additional accommodation and the advantage to the landlord exceeds the tenant's hardship, the landlord is entitled to an eviction order.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in revision with an appellate authority's findings when those findings result from failure to consider relevant evidence or application of wrong tests.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found in favour of the landlords on comparative hardship.
The Appellate Authority reversed that finding without due regard to relevant evidence and applied wrong tests.
The High Court restored the Rent Controller's eviction order in revision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to allow the revision because the Appellate Authority's findings were vitiated by its failure to consider evidence and its errors in assessing comparative hardship.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 permits revisional interference where the appellate authority's decision is affected by manifest errors in the exercise of its jurisdiction, including failure to advert to relevant evidence or application of wrong tests.

predicates.rent_control_revision_proceeding: A party seeks High Court revision of an appellate decision in a rent-control matter.
predicates.appellate_authority_failed_to_consider_r: The appellate authority did not consider evidence relevant to its decision.
predicates.appellate_authority_applied_wrong_test: The appellate authority assessed the issue using an incorrect test.

issues.definition: In a rent-control revision, the High Court may interfere when the appellate authority failed to consider relevant evidence and applied an incorrect test.

issues.legal_issue: A predecessor's unsuccessful eviction proceeding does not by itself establish that a successor landlord's claim for eviction is mala fide.
material_facts: The former owner had earlier brought an unsuccessful eviction suit against the tenant.
The present landlords acquired the property as legatees and later sought eviction for additional accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The former owner's unsuccessful eviction suit did not make the legatee landlords' claim mala fide.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the motives of successor landlords cannot be treated as mala fide merely because their predecessor in title had previously brought an unsuccessful eviction suit.

predicates.successor_landlord_seeks_eviction: A person who succeeded to ownership seeks eviction of a tenant.
predicates.predecessor_brought_unsuccessful_evictio: A former owner previously brought an eviction suit against the same tenant and did not succeed.

issues.definition: A successor landlord's eviction claim is not shown to be mala fide solely because a former owner brought an unsuccessful eviction suit.
